text: In the late 19th century Spanish Philippines,
society held a very specific standard for women of wealth.
You were expected to be quiet, heavily refined,
and confine your entire existence to the domestic spaces of the home.
Teresa Magbanua rejected that standard from the start.
As a young girl in Ilo Ilo,
she preferred climbing trees,
swimming across rivers,
and wrestling in the dirt with her brothers,
overlearning embroidery or polite conversation.
Hoping to instill some traditional grace into their daughter,
her affluent parents sent her away.
They enrolled her in a series of highly prestigious,
all-girls Catholic schools in the capital,
to smooth out her rough edges.
This photograph shows the Escoulta,
the bustling cosmopolitan thoroughfare of Manila at the time.
Here, at the epicenter of Philippine high society,
Teresa immersed herself in an elite academic environment,
eventually earning a master's degree.
But the capital didn't tame her spirit,
it sharpened her intellect.
She returned to her hometown not as a docile socialite,
but as a fiercely strict, highly respected schoolteacher,
whose discipline demanded absolute attention
from her classroom.
Eventually, Teresa stepped away from the blackboard.
She married a wealthy landowner named Alejandro Balderos,
retiring from education to help manage
his vast agricultural properties in the town of Sarra.
Running those expansive farms
required a different set of disciplines,
to oversee the massive estates,
she lured to ride a horse
across long stretches of rugged terrain.
And to protect herself in the countryside,
she mastered firing a pistol.
You can see the heavy determination
in this archival photograph
of lightly equipped Filipino revolutionary soldiers
gathering for war.
In 1896, the Philippine Revolution
against the Spanish Empire erupted,
calling citizens across the islands to arms.
Teresa immediately wanted to enlist in the fight.
Her husband, however, issued a flat refusal,
insisting that the battlefield
was absolutely no place for a woman.
The revolutionary forces were desperately short
on capable, disciplined leadership,
yet the prevailing culture dictated
that a highly competent, sharp-shooting former teacher
had to sit out the war simply because she was a wife.
Teresa ignored him entirely.
She saddled her horse and rode hard,
directly to the revolutionary headquarters in Panay.
When she arrived, she presented herself
to the commanding officer of the Northern Zone,
General Perfecto Poblador,
who also happened to be her uncle.
He immediately denied her request
for a military commission, citing her gender.
She didn't argue the point with words.
Teresa grabbed a weapon, stepped onto the firing line,
and decisively outshot the general's own enlisted men
in a public display of marksmanship.
Faced with that undeniable display
of elite skill, the general caved.
He handed his niece a commission
that defied every rule of the era,
command over an entire battalion of men
armed with bolos, or heavy machetes.
She bypassed the military patriarchy
by removing their ability to say no.
By deploying overwhelming, undeniable competence,
she left the establishment with no logical choice
but to follow her lead.
Her combat debut immediately proved the general right.
At Barrio Yating, Teresa personally led
a ferocious cavalry charge, plunging into the Spanish lines
armed with a pistol in one hand and a bolo in the other.
Her true test arrived shortly after
at the Battle of Sapong Hills.
Her unit faced a heavily armed Spanish colonial force
that held superior weapons,
had better training, and the high ground.
On this map of Sapong Hills,
red blocks mark fortified Spanish positions.
To neutralize them, Teresa orchestrates
a rapid flanking maneuver.
Blue arrows, representing her forces,
navigate steep terrain to strike from unexpected angles.
Her disciplined troops perfectly synchronize their attack,
collapsing on the red blocks and forcing retreat.
That brilliant tactical victory earned her
the absolute loyalty of her troops,
who lovingly bestowed her with the title
Ne-isa, or Mother-isa.
It proved that managing a rigid classroom
was the perfect primer for controlling
the chaos of a battlefield.
The Spanish eventually ceded the Philippines,
but the war didn't end.
The United States immediately arrived to occupy the islands,
forcing Teresa to transition her men
into a grueling, attritional guerrilla campaign.
This photograph shows American soldiers
firing from a fortified trench.
At battles like Balantung,
Teresa's forces faced industrialized fire power
and superior logistics.
Yet, the heaviest flows she absorbed
didn't come from foreign artillery.
Her two brothers, Generals Pasquale and Elias,
were assassinated by rival, in-fighting Filipino factions.
By 1901, stripped of her family
and commanding a starving, depleted force
with no remaining ammunition,
she made the agonizing decision to disband her troops
and send the survivors home.
She relinquished her army,
but she refused to yield her ideology.
Teresa flatly rejected the mandatory oath of allegiance,
keeping her unsurrendered spirit entirely intact.
40 years later, the world plunged into the Second World War.
Teresa was an elderly widow in her 70s,
removed from the battlefields of her youth.
Then, a third major global empire threatened her home.
This photograph captures a Japanese soldier
patrolling a civilian street
during the occupation of the Philippines.
She could no longer lead a cavalry charge,
so she fought from the shadows.
She quietly sold off her remaining personal properties
and lifelong heirlooms,
funneling the funds directly to the local guerrilla resistance.
By the time the war ended,
her military resume stood practically alone in history.
She actively resisted three consecutive global empires
in a single lifetime.
The Visayan Joan of Arc never waited
for society's permission to fight for her country.
She proved that true leadership
relies entirely on absolute competence.
And in doing so, she left behind a multi-generational lesson
in unsurrendered courage.
